sections.heading: Can Infrared Technology Detect Roof Leaks? Limits of Infrared Thermography

runs.v: Infrared technology detects roof leaks by the hidden moisture they leave behind: moisture intrusion leaves moisture trapped in the insulation, and water trapped beneath a roofing membrane has a much higher thermal capacity than dry insulation, so it adds thermal mass. After a sunny day the wet areas retain heat longer than the dry areas during cooling and show at night as thermal anomalies, distinct hot spots on the scan. Thermal imaging cameras capture those surface temperature anomalies that indicate moisture presence, reading temperature differences across the whole roof surface, high-resolution infrared cameras detect subtle thermal patterns, and the image appears instantly as the technician walks, although each anomaly still has to be verified. Infrared cameras reveal leak patterns invisible to the naked eye, including leaks that surface nowhere near the source of the water intrusion, where traditional inspection methods, such as walking the membrane or probing it square by square, miss trapped moisture the human eye cannot see.

infrared scans can catch moisture before it causes indoor leaks or structural damage, and routine infrared scans can help prevent mold growth and protect buildings against weather fluctuations. The infrared inspection is non-invasive; it helps technicians accurately identify the boundaries of wet insulation, confirmed by core cuts, and flags potential problems at drains and seams before a small leak becomes extensive damage. That reduces unnecessary repairs, prevents water damage, and saves money on the job. Saturated insulation also loses much of its insulating value and drives heat loss, so replacing only the wet boards helps restore energy efficiency.

The method depends on the operator's expertise more than on the equipment: a certified specialist should have rigorous training and relevant qualifications, thermographers need years of experience to interpret an image properly, a qualified thermographer uses high-quality calibrated equipment, and any professional doing the work should be familiar with both infrared thermography and moisture meters. That holds whether the camera is handheld or on a drone: there is no single best drone for roof inspections, and any aerial scan needs a radiometric thermal camera, an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot, and the same night-time conditions.

faqs.q: How does infrared roof leak detection find a leak on a Bloomfield roof?

runs.v: It scans the roof after sunset and maps the subsurface wet insulation, which retains solar heat longer than dry insulation and shows as a warm anomaly on the thermal image. Wet insulation carries higher heat capacity and cools more slowly, per Fluke and IIBEC, and ASTM C1153 names this the standard practice for locating wet insulation, per ASTM and the NRCA.

faqs.q: Does infrared imaging find the exact leak entry point?

runs.v: No. Infrared imaging locates the wet insulation, not the leak entry point itself, because water travels through the roof assembly and the wet area separates from the breach, per Fluke and IIBEC. The verified wet area is then traced back toward the flashing detail that admits the water.

faqs.q: Why does ASTM C1153 require a core cut on my Bloomfield commercial roof?

runs.v: A thermal anomaly indicates suspected moisture rather than a diagnosis, so ASTM C1153 requires every suspected wet area be verified by core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter, which confirms the presence, depth, and extent of the moisture, per ASTM and Fluke. The check matters most in winter, when the wet-area contrast narrows to about 5°F against 20°F in summer, per IIBEC and Fluke.
